lesson_title: The League Table That Predicts Every Battery
hook_text: Chemistry published a league table that calls the winner of every electron fight — before it happens.
clip_script: Why is it always zinc that dissolves and copper that plates — never the other way? Because the contest was decided before the beakers were filled. Chemistry keeps a published ranking of electron grabbers: the table of standard electrode potentials. Top of the log, with big positive voltages, the ruthless grabbers — fluorine is the reigning champion, unbeaten. Bottom of the log, the soft touches — lithium and potassium, metals that practically post their electrons away. Every number answers one question: measured against hydrogen, the agreed zero of the sport, how hard does this species pull on electrons? Match any two entries and the result is fixed: the higher-ranked side grabs and is reduced, the lower-ranked side surrenders and is oxidised. And the table even publishes the final score in advance — the gap between the two rankings is the cell's voltage. Copper against zinc: a gap of one comma one volts, a middleweight contest. Silver against aluminium: two comma four six volts, a rout. This is exactly how battery designers work — they scan the table for wide gaps between materials that are also cheap and safe, because the gap IS the number printed on the battery. One page of rankings, and every electron fight on Earth is called before kick-off.
visual_style: A sports league log whose entries are chemical species with voltages as points; two rows highlighted and pulled out to face each other; the gap between them stretching into a glowing voltage readout on a battery label.
mood: Sports-commentary energy applied to chemistry — confident, predictive, a table that never loses a bet.
pacing: Rhetorical question opener, league-table reveal, two quick match-ups with scores, designer's-secret close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read the table like a fixture list in your final exams.
